The raytracing performance is still not quite powerful enough to really show it's potential yet, but the movie industry would kill for any hardware accelerated raytracing, if the rendering software is updated to take advantage of it then nVidia is going to have a massive new market for it's RTX cards.
The other factor is that while it might not be good now nVidia has working chips in consumers hands that they can gather data and improve upon so by the time it is a widely sought after feature AMD could be too far behind to catch up so they are still going to need to contend with it as soon as possible so they don't get left behind.
author: @AusSkiller

text: @AusSkiller  The movie industry isn't going to make use of RTX cards. They have much more powerful solutions already. RTX isn't even fully rendering using ray tracing, it's a hybrid but still using mostly rasterization. It also slows down performance by a lot. Most gamers will try it then promptly disable it. It's not going to be a purchasing factor for most people. By the time it's a feature in mass use, there will be much more powerful cards out. Like i said, you won't be using a gen 1 RTX card by that time.
author: @KBW19723

text:
@KBW19723  Pretty much all raytracing is done in software at the moment, and CPUs are god awful slow for something like that, which means movie studios end up using a farm of PCs to get the kind of performance they need. Hardware dedicated to a type of work is many many times faster than software, that's exactly why no one uses software rendering anymore and why ASICs are so much better at mining crypto-currency. And while you are correct that RTX uses rasterisation too it doesn't mean it cannot be used for movie raytracing. At the very least it could be used as a more accurate previs pass, but given the rasterisation is simply an optimisation for games to run at better frame rates I don't see why you couldn't use more rays to get movie accurate results instead just at a MUCH lower frame rate.
But only time will tell, raytracing is the inevitable way forward and it is undeniable that nVidia has the leg up at this point. Though I absolutely agree that for gamers it really shouldn't be much of a consideration with the 20xx cards as the benefits are currently too minimal to justify it.

It actually is a smaller process, while some elements remain similar, densities can be greater.
It's still all part of "14nm" but how much you get out of it depends on how you design it.

When AMD took Zen+ to 12nm, they basically just adapted the 14nm layout rather than do a complete redesign to take advantage of the shrunken components. They basically just swapped out the bigger transistors for the smaller while leaving everything else in place, they could have achieved a 10-20% die shrink, but likely deemed the additional work to redesign either not worth it or would take too many resources to do for only marginal overall gains to yield due to the shrink savings.

There's not a lot of info on TSMC's density improvements over 16nm, but it should be in that 10-20% range. Especially considering that Pascal was made with earlier 16nm processes. 

"which is an optimized version of the company’s CLN16FFC that is set to use 6T libraries (as opposed to 7.5T and 9T libraries) providing a 20% area reduction. "
